Choose a Koh Samui sanctuary where visitors watch, walk beside and feed retired elephants but never ride or bathe them; that rules out several well-known names. Half-day visits with hotel transfer and a meal cost about 3,000 THB per adult and 1,500 THB per child in 2026, short 1–1.5 hour visits 1,000–2,000 THB. Only one Samui venue, with sites in the Bophut hills and above Chaweng Noi, is listed as high-welfare by World Animal Protection, and no venue on the island meets the strictest standard because all of them include hand-feeding. Below we explain the trade-offs and what we will and won't sell.

What "ethical" means on Koh Samui

An ethical venue puts the elephants' needs before the visitors' photos. In practice that means no riding of any kind, no bathing or mud-bathing with visitors, no hooks (ankus) or chains used to control the animals, no shows, painting or tricks, no breeding of baby elephants to attract visitors, and small groups that watch from a respectful distance. Elephants there should spend most of the day doing what elephants do: foraging, dust-bathing, wallowing in mud and socialising, not standing in line for selfies. World Animal Protection's position is simple: no responsible venue breeds elephants for tourism, and the best visits are observation-only.

Why we don't sell elephant riding

An elephant only lets people ride it after it has been trained to submit, and that training traditionally involves separating young elephants from their mothers and breaking their will. Seats strapped to an elephant's back also press on a spine that isn't built to carry weight from above. "Short", "bareback" or "neck" rides are still rides. We don't sell them, we don't link to venues that offer them, and we don't use photos of them.

Why bathing with elephants is off our list

Bathing with elephants looks gentle, but it puts groups of tourists in the water with animals that weigh several tonnes, and it usually means the elephants are walked into the river or pool on command, several times a day, whether they want to or not. The welfare standards we follow treat tourist bathing as close contact that needs control of the animal. Elephants bathe and mud-wallow very happily on their own; the better venues let you watch that from the bank or a platform.

Feeding: the honest trade-off

Every elephant venue on Samui includes some hand-feeding of fruit, vegetables or rice balls, and the strictest welfare standard excludes even that, because it encourages elephants to approach people. So no Samui venue meets the very top standard. We think a short, supervised feeding session at a no-riding, no-bathing sanctuary is an acceptable compromise for most families: it pays for the elephants' care and keeps them out of riding camps. If you want the purest option, choose the observation-only skywalk visit below.

How to check a sanctuary: 7 questions

  1. Is there any riding, at any time of day? If yes, walk away.
  2. Do visitors bathe, shower or mud-bathe with the elephants? It should be no.
  3. Do keepers carry hooks, or are elephants chained during visiting hours? Neither should be visible.
  4. Are there shows, painting, football or tricks? Any trick means training by force.
  5. Are there baby elephants? Ask where they came from. Breeding for tourism is a red flag.
  6. How many visitors per session? Smaller groups mean calmer elephants.
  7. Is the venue listed by a welfare organisation? World Animal Protection and Responsible Travel publish the venues they support.

Red flags on the day

  • Elephants standing on concrete in the sun, or swaying and bobbing their heads repeatedly (a stress behaviour).
  • Keepers hiding hooks behind their backs or in a bag when visitors arrive.
  • An elephant tied up beside a car park or viewpoint for feeding photos.
  • "Sanctuary" on the sign but riding seats stacked behind the shed.
  • Pressure to pay extra for close-up photos or a ride "just for the children".

If you see something that worries you, leave, don't pay for extras, and tell us so we can take it up with the venue.

Where Samui's elephants come from

Most elephants in Thai tourism were once working animals. When Thailand banned commercial logging in 1989, thousands of elephants and their mahouts lost their work, and many moved into tourism: trekking, riding, shows and street begging. Samui's elephants came to the island this way. Today a sanctuary usually buys or leases elephants from riding camps, and the money visitors pay covers food, vets and keepers for animals that can live 60 years or more. That is why the choice of venue matters: your ticket keeps an elephant either in a better life or in the old one.

Venue policies change, so ask us before you book if one of these points matters to you.

Programmes differ more than the names suggest. The 1-hour "feeding visits" are mainly food preparation and hand-feeding, with little time to watch the elephants behave naturally. The 3-hour half days add a walk with or behind the herd and time to watch them forage, dust-bathe and wallow, which is where you learn most. One Bophut sanctuary also runs a full-day volunteer programme, 09:00–16:00, for up to 6 people at about 6,500 THB, with food preparation and work around the park but no bathing. If you have the time, a half day is the better visit for you and the elephants: the money supports the same care, and the animals spend more of your visit doing what they choose.

Places we would skip

  • Roadside feeding stops, such as the elephant-feeding add-on on the way up to Overlap Stone, where young elephants have been reported kept on chains.
  • The elephant attractions on the Na Muang waterfall road, including the site at the address of the former safari park, where older listings still describe riding and shows. Until the riding question is settled, we don't promote it. If you visit Na Muang Waterfall, use the waterfall's own car park.
  • Any "bathing" or "shower" programme, however gentle it looks in photos.
  • Venues with baby elephants and no clear story of where they came from.

Elephant feeding on a 4x4 safari

Two of our full-day jungle safaris include a stop to prepare food for and hand-feed elephants, with no riding or bathing: the 4x4 safari with elephant feeding (1,950 / 1,450 THB) and the jungle safari with elephant feeding (2,000 / 1,500 THB). They suit families who want waterfalls, temples and elephants in one day. The elephant part is short, though, and these are not sanctuary visits. If welfare is your priority, book a dedicated sanctuary visit instead of the short elephant-camp add-ons that some sightseeing tours offer.

Prices in 2026

On Samui, a 3-hour half-day visit with transfer and a meal costs about 3,000 THB per adult and 1,500 THB per child, and short 1–1.5 hour visits cost 1,000–2,000 THB. Our visits cost 1,000–3,500 THB per adult and 500–2,000 THB per child, depending on length, meal and transfer. Free ages and child bands differ: most venues let children under 4 in free and charge the child price from 4 or 5 to 11. Be wary of much cheaper offers: a ticket of a few hundred baht usually buys a short feeding stop, not a sanctuary visit.

Visiting with children

Children love elephant visits, and the best venues are good at explaining why the elephants are there. Child prices on our visits run from 500 THB (the 1-hour feed-and-walk visit) to 2,000 THB (the half-day museum programmes), and children under 4 visit free at most sanctuaries; the age at which the adult price starts is 12 at most venues. Babies and toddlers are easiest on the short and observation-only visits; bring a carrier rather than a pushchair, as paths are uneven. The 3-hour walks suit children who can walk on rough paths for 30–45 minutes. Hold small children's hands near the elephants, and let them feed from a platform or with a keeper beside them. The short 1.5-hour visit and the skywalk visit are the easiest with under-6s. For more family ideas see things to do on Koh Samui.

Staying safe around elephants

  • Follow the keepers' instructions at all times; they know each elephant's mood.
  • Never walk directly behind an elephant or between a mother and calf.
  • Offer food with a flat palm or by placing it in the trunk as shown, then step back.
  • No sudden movements, shouting, flash photography or selfie sticks close to the animals.
  • Stay out of the mud pools and the river: that space is the elephants'.

What to wear and bring

  • Clothes you don't mind getting muddy, or the shirts some venues lend.
  • Closed shoes or sandals with straps; paths are uneven and slippery after rain.
  • Insect repellent, sunscreen and a hat.
  • A change of clothes for the drive back.
  • Cash for drinks, souvenirs and tips for the keepers.

Morning or afternoon, and which season

Morning sessions are cooler for people and elephants, and the elephants are often more active. Afternoon sessions are quieter and suit late risers. Visits run all year. From October to December expect showers and mud: the sanctuaries keep going in rain, the paths get slippery, and the elephants enjoy the mud wallows most. A light rain jacket is more useful than an umbrella around large animals. From March to May it is hottest, often 32–33 °C by midday, so take the morning slot and drink plenty. A sanctuary visit is also a good choice on days when the sea is too rough for a boat trip, which is common on the east coast in November and December. Check the forecast: [kp_weather_now]

Transfers and getting there

Most visits include return transfer from the main beach areas (Chaweng, Lamai, Bophut, Maenam, Choeng Mon and Bang Rak); steep hillside villas usually get a nearby meeting point or a small surcharge, confirmed before you book. The 1-hour feed-and-walk visit has no transfer. The sanctuaries are in the hills above Bophut, above Chaweng Noi and inland at Na Mueang; we send the exact pin with your confirmation. If you drive yourself, the last stretch to the hillside sanctuaries is steep and narrow: a car is fine in dry weather, but don't ride a rental scooter up after rain.

Photos and behaviour

Good sanctuaries let you take as many photos as you like from where you stand, without staged poses. Don't ask keepers to make an elephant lift its trunk or "smile"; that is a trained trick. Don't fly drones near the animals. Share your photos with the venue's name and the words "no riding": it helps other travellers choose well.

Questions to ask before you book any elephant visit

Whether you book with us or anyone else, these questions sort the sanctuaries from the camps in a minute:

  • How many elephants live there, and where did each one come from?
  • Are any elephants ridden, bathed with visitors or used in shows, at this site or a sister site?
  • How many visitors join each session?
  • Where are the elephants at night, and are they chained?
  • Does the price include transfer and a meal, and is there anything to pay on the day?

A good sanctuary answers all five without hesitation. Vague answers about where the elephants came from, or a "special" ride offered on arrival, tell you all you need to know.

What we will never sell

  • Elephant riding of any length, with or without a seat
  • Bathing, showering or mud-bathing with elephants
  • Elephant shows, painting or football
  • Roadside feeding of chained elephants
  • Photo props with baby elephants, monkeys, snakes or tigers
